data.title: What Are Human Rights?
data.sourcePassage: Human rights are protections every person is entitled to simply by being human, regardless of their race, religion, gender, nationality, or any other characteristic. The modern human rights framework was established after the horrors of the Second World War. In 1948, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), setting out the basic rights every person should enjoy. These include the right to life, the right to education, freedom of religion or belief, and the right to seek asylum from persecution. Human rights are closely connected to the concept of dignity — the intrinsic worth and value of every person. It is important to distinguish between equality and equity: equality means giving everyone the same basic respect and opportunities, while equity means giving people what they specifically need for fair outcomes, which may differ between individuals. Rights and responsibilities are two sides of the same coin: having rights means others have responsibilities towards you, and exercising your rights means accepting responsibilities towards others.

data.title: Religious Foundations for Human Dignity
data.sourcePassage: Many religious traditions provide their own foundations for the belief that every person has dignity and deserves to be treated with respect. Christianity and Judaism teach that all humans are made 'in the image of God' — a concept known as imago Dei. Because every person carries this divine quality, every person has inherent worth. Islam teaches that Allah has honoured all children of Adam, and that humans are khalifah — stewards of God's creation — with responsibilities towards all people. Sikhism declares that there is one God (Ik Onkar) and therefore one human family — Guru Nanak taught that there is but one race, the human race. Hinduism teaches that the divine (Brahman) is present in every person, and the principle of ahimsa (non-violence) requires respect for all living beings. Buddhism grounds human dignity in compassion (karuna) — the wish for all beings to be free from suffering. Humanism provides a non-religious foundation: human dignity and wellbeing matter because of our shared humanity and capacity for reason and empathy, not because of God. While these foundations differ, they reach a similar conclusion: all people matter and must be treated with respect.

data.title: Prejudice, Discrimination, and Refugees
data.sourcePassage: Prejudice is an unfair, pre-formed opinion about a group of people without knowledge or evidence. When someone acts on prejudice by treating a person unfairly because of who they are, this is discrimination. A stereotype is an oversimplified, fixed image of a group that ignores individual differences. In Britain, the law protects people from discrimination on the basis of protected characteristics — including age, disability, gender, race, religion, and sexual orientation. Specific forms of religious prejudice include Islamophobia (prejudice against Muslims) and antisemitism (prejudice against Jewish people). The UDHR Article 14 protects the right to seek asylum. A refugee is a person who has been formally recognised as having fled persecution and has legal protections under the 1951 UN Refugee Convention. An asylum seeker is someone who has applied for this protection but whose claim has not yet been assessed — the two terms are often confused. Religious communities have strong traditions of welcoming the stranger: Christianity teaches love of the stranger; gurdwaras provide shelter and food to all; and Islam emphasises protection of those in need.

questions.question: What is the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
options: They mean the same thing
Prejudice is an unfair opinion; discrimination is acting on that opinion
Discrimination is about speech; prejudice is about actions
Prejudice is illegal; discrimination is sometimes allowed

questions.question: What is a protected characteristic?
options: A religious symbol worn in public
A quality the law protects from discrimination, such as religion or race
A type of human right not listed in the UDHR
A characteristic only relevant in criminal law

questions.question: What is the difference between an asylum seeker and a refugee?
options: A refugee has fled their country; an asylum seeker has not
An asylum seeker's claim is being assessed; a refugee has been formally recognised and given protection
A refugee is only protected in Europe; an asylum seeker has global protection

questions.question: What is antisemitism?

Opposition to all forms of religious belief
